title: Health checks (/health, readiness vs liveness)
hook: Health check endpoints tell orchestrators whether your API is alive and ready to receive traffic. Kubernetes uses separate liveness and readiness probes — confusing them causes pods killed during startup or traffic routed to broken instances.

blocks.text: ASP.NET Core health checks (`AddHealthChecks`, `MapHealthChecks`) expose HTTP endpoints that run registered IHealthCheck implementations and return Healthy, Degraded, or Unhealthy with optional JSON details. Liveness probes answer 'is the process hung?' — failure restarts the pod. Readiness probes answer 'can this instance handle requests?' — failure removes it from the load balancer without restart. Startup probes give slow-starting apps extra time before liveness kicks in. Built-in checks cover SQL Server, Redis, and URL groups; custom checks validate your critical dependencies.

entries.plainDefinition: Checks if the container is running; failure triggers pod restart. Should be lightweight — not depend on external DB.
Checks if instance can serve traffic; failure removes from Service endpoints without restart.
Custom check returning HealthCheckResult with status and description.
entries.example: CheckHealthAsync returns Unhealthy if Redis down

entries.plainDefinition: Optional dashboard package aggregating multiple service health endpoints — dev/staging, not for public prod.

blocks.text: A common production incident: readiness check includes database, database blips, Kubernetes marks all pods NotReady, Service has zero endpoints — full outage. Another trap: liveness check hits the database; slow DB causes liveness failure → restart loop. Senior engineers design three endpoints (/health/live, /health/ready, optional /health/startup), keep liveness dumb (self-check only), put dependency checks on readiness, and exclude health paths from authentication and heavy tracing.

blocks.title: Liveness = restart, readiness = route traffic
blocks.body: Never put external dependency checks on liveness — transient DB outage should not kill your pod. Readiness failure is recoverable when the dependency returns.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Pod starts, startup probe runs (optional)
items.body: Allows 60+ seconds for EF migrations or cache warm-up before liveness applies.

items.title: Readiness fails during warm-up
items.body: Pod running but not in Service endpoints — no traffic yet.

items.title: Readiness passes
items.body: Pod receives traffic from Ingress/Service load balancer.

items.title: Liveness runs periodically
items.body: Lightweight self-check; deadlock or hung thread pool → restart.

items.title: Readiness fails on dependency loss
items.body: Pod removed from LB; process keeps running; recovers when DB returns.

diagram.title: Liveness vs readiness in Kubernetes

snippet.label: Register health checks with tags
snippet.code:
builder.Services.AddHealthChecks()
    .AddCheck("self", () => HealthCheckResult.Healthy(), tags: ["live"])
    .AddNpgSql(builder.Configuration.GetConnectionString("OrdersDb")!,
        name: "postgres", tags: ["ready"])
    .AddRedis(builder.Configuration["Redis:Connection"]!,
        name: "redis-cache", tags: ["ready"])
    .AddUrlGroup(new Uri("https://payments.internal/health"),
        name: "payments-api", tags: ["ready"]);
snippet.explanation: Tags partition checks into liveness (self only) and readiness (dependencies). AddNpgSql runs SELECT 1 — keep timeout short (2-3 seconds).

snippet.label: Map separate liveness and readiness endpoints
snippet.explanation: Predicate filters which checks run per endpoint. Degraded as 200 is a team choice — document it. Kubernetes expects 200 healthy, non-200 unhealthy.

snippet.label: Kubernetes deployment probes
snippet.code:
spec:
  containers:
  - name: orders-api
    livenessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /health/live
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 10
      periodSeconds: 15
      failureThreshold: 3
    readinessProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /health/ready
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 10
      failureThreshold: 2
    startupProbe:
      httpGet:
        path: /health/ready
        port: 8080
      failureThreshold: 30
      periodSeconds: 5
snippet.explanation: startupProbe allows 30×5s = 150s warm-up before liveness kills the pod. readinessProbe failureThreshold 2 removes pod quickly from LB on DB failure.

snippet.label: Custom health check with timeout and cache
snippet.explanation: Always timeout external checks — hung health check hangs the probe and cascades. Register with tags: ['ready'] only, never 'live'.

blocks.title: Health endpoints: Express vs ASP.NET Core
Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Single /health endpoint used for both liveness and readiness with DB check — causes restart loops. Health checks behind JWT authentication — K8s probes get 401. Heavy work in health checks (full table scan). Not using startupProbe for slow EF migrations. Health check spam in traces and logs — exclude /health from OTel and reduce logging.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: kubectl describe pod shows Last State and probe failure messages. Simulate readiness failure by blocking DB network policy — pods should go NotReady without restart. Simulate liveness failure only with a deliberate deadlock test in staging. Degraded status is useful for non-critical dependency failure (recommendation engine down) while core API stays ready — document team policy. Health Checks UI is great for ops dashboards in staging; in prod use Prometheus blackbox exporter or synthetic monitors. Align probe timeouts with health check CancellationToken — K8s timeoutSeconds must exceed your slowest ready check.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying liveness and readiness are the same endpoint with the same checks. Putting database on liveness probe. Not knowing K8s removes NotReady pods from Service endpoints without restarting. Unable to explain startupProbe purpose for slow-starting .NET apps with migrations.

interviewTakeaways: Health checks expose HTTP endpoints; liveness = restart if hung, readiness = route traffic only if dependencies ok.
Tradeoff: strict readiness (many deps) improves traffic quality but increases blast radius when shared DB blips — mark non-critical deps Degraded.
Production tip: /health/live tags ['live'] self only; /health/ready tags ['ready'] for DB/Redis; AllowAnonymous; startupProbe for migrations.

60s: AddHealthChecks with tags. MapHealthChecks separate live and ready paths. K8s liveness restarts pod. Readiness removes from load balancer. Never DB on liveness. startupProbe for slow boot. Exclude from auth and tracing.
Follow-up: what happens if all pods fail readiness simultaneously during a database outage?
commonPitfalls: Saying 'one /health endpoint is enough for Kubernetes' gets you rejected — liveness and readiness have different failure actions.
Database check on liveness — transient outage kills all pods in restart loop instead of graceful traffic drain.
Strong answer: 'Tagged checks, separate endpoints, liveness is dumb self-check, readiness validates deps, startupProbe for EF migrations, 503 on unhealthy ready, probes unauthenticated.'
introducedIn: ASP.NET Core 2.2 AddHealthChecks; Kubernetes probe patterns platform-agnostic
